hooks.text: You can see one impossible galaxy through the gap of another.
Why is there a second galaxy hidden inside this cosmic smoke ring?
One impossible ring galaxy is hiding another six hundred million light-years away.

title: The Impossible Ring Inside Hoag's Object
description: Astronomer Arthur Hoag found a galaxy that shouldn't exist, only to find another one hidden inside it.

beats.text: You can see one impossible galaxy through the gap of another.
beats.visual: Hubble Space Telescope wide view of Hoag's Object, 2001

beats.text: In 1950, Arthur Hoag found a blue smoke ring around a golden core in the Serpens constellation.
beats.visual: star chart showing the Serpens constellation

beats.text: Hoag first thought this bizarre structure was a simple planetary nebula or a gas cloud.
beats.visual: Hubble image of the Ring Nebula M57, 1998

beats.text: He even guessed it was an optical illusion caused by gravity bending distant light.
beats.visual: diagram showing gravitational lensing of a distant galaxy

beats.text: But Hoag's Object is a real galaxy, six hundred million light-years away and wider than the Milky Way.
beats.visual: High-resolution Hubble image of Hoag's Object nucleus and ring
queries: Hoag's Object Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2

beats.text: Most ring galaxies form from violent collisions, yet no crash site exists here.
beats.visual: Hubble image of the Cartwheel Galaxy showing collision evidence

beats.text: Peering through the dark gap at the one o’clock position reveals a one-in-a-million photobomb.
beats.visual: Cropped Hubble image of Hoag's Object focusing on the 1 o'clock gap

beats.text: Deep in the background sits another ring galaxy perfectly aligned with the first.
beats.visual: Extreme zoom on the background ring galaxy within the gap

beats.text: It is the only place where you can see one impossible galaxy through the gap of another.
beats.visual: Full view of Hoag's Object showing both rings
